Here’s a structured 12-week upper-body strength program tailored for a 29-year-old recreational climber with right subacromial impingement, cleared for pain-free range and no overhead loading. She’s four months into physio, so we’ll emphasize scapular control, rotator cuff/periscapular strengthening, controlled pushing/pulling patterns, and gradual loading with a focus on pain-free moving patterns. The program assumes access to a full gym and requires clinician clearance if any pain flares.

Overall plan
- Phases: 4 phases of 3 weeks each, with specific goals and progressions.
- Weekly structure: 3 non-consecutive upper-body days plus one optional accessory day; 1 low-load, high-rep mobility/technique day integrated as needed.
- Core pillars: scapular stability, rotator cuff strengthening, eccentrics, slow tempo for tendon health, gradual introduction of resistance with pain-free ROM only.
- Climbing transfer: build pulling strength, grip endurance, and upper-back engagement while limiting overhead loading. Use horizontal pulls and controlled pressing within pain-free range.

Key cues and safety
- Arm position: avoid end-range overhead loading. Prioritize scapular retraction/depression and humeral neutral or slight external rotation.
- Pain rule: if pain > 2/10 or mechanical catching, stop and modify to a pain-free ROM or regression.
- Warm-up: 10–12 minutes prior to sessions including scapular floor slides, band dislocates (light), rotator cuff activation, and thoracic mobility.
- Progression: follow weekly load increases only if the technique is pain-free and performance targets are met.

Phase 1 (Weeks 1–3): Foundation and hinge on pain-free ROM, scapular control
 goals: establish consistent scapular motor control, rotator cuff endurance, and build confidence with loading in pain-free ranges.
 Weekly template (3 days; Day A, B, C)
- Day A: Horizontal pulling focus + supporting pressing mobility
  1) Warm-up: scapular band pull-aparts 2 x 15; rotator cuff activation: sidelying external rotation 2 x 12 per side; thoracic rotation mobility 2 x 8 per side.
  2) Dumbbell bench press (flat) or floor press: 3 x 10–12 (control tempo 3–0-1-0; light weight)
  3) Barbell or dumbbell row (supported torso) or chest-supported row: 3 x 8–12
  4) Seated cable face pulls: 3 x 12–15
  5) Dumbbell anti-rotational press (rotator cuff friendly) or presses in neutral grip with short ROM: 2–3 x 8–10
  6) Core: dead bug or paloff press 3 x 10–12 (light)
  7) Mobility/finish: lat stretch, pec minor stretch 2 x 30s

- Day B: Pulling strength with scapular emphasis
  1) Warm-up as above
  2) Lat pulldown (neutral or supinated grip) to chest height only if pain-free; 3 x 8–10
  3) Seated cable row or incline row: 3 x 8–12
  4) Dumbbell rear delt row or band pull-aparts: 3 x 12
  5) Pronated grip isn’t required; opt for neutral grip to reduce impingement risk
  6) Co-contraction work: prone Y-raises on table with light dumbbells 2 x 12
  7) Mobility: doorway pec stretch 2 x 30s; thoracic extension on foam roller 2 x 1 min

- Day C: Push with control and rotator cuff care
  1) Warm-up: 2–3 rounds of shoulder-friendly activation
  2) Push-up variation on elevated surface (to reduce ROM) or machine chest press: 3 x 8–12
  3) Dumbbell incline press (limited angle, pain-free range): 3 x 8–12
  4) Cable or band internal/external rotation at 0–45 degrees abduction: 3 x 12–15
  5) Scapular push-ups or floor scapular slides: 3 x 12–15
  6) Anti-rotator cuff walkouts or anti-extension with band: 2 x 10
  7) Mobility: scapular wall slides 2 x 10; doorway stretch 2 x 30s

- Progression cues for Phase 1:
  - Increase total volume gradually if no pain and technique is solid. Target a small load increase each week on main lifts, staying within 1–2 reps of failure or at ~75–80% of baseline effort.
  - If any pain arises in overhead components, regress to neutral/grip-closed positions, reduce ROM, or switch to machine-based alternatives.

Phase 2 (Weeks 4–6): Building strength with controlled progression and safe overload
 goals: incrementally increase loading, refine scapular mechanics, and introduce more pulling volume with minimal overhead pressing.
 Weekly template (3 days; Day A, B, C)
- Day A: Horizontal push/pull and scapular stability
  1) Warm-up: same as Phase 1 with added banded scapular pulls
  2) Barbell or dumbbell bench press: 4 x 6–8 (control tempo 3–0-1-0; moderate weight)
  3) Barbell or Dumbbell row (bent over but supported with torso or chest-supported row): 4 x 6–8
  4) Inverted row or supported T-bar row: 3 x 8–12
  5) Cable face pulls: 3 x 12–15
  6) Pallof press: 3 x 12 each side
  7) Mobility/soft tissue: pec minor stretch; thoracic sufficiency

- Day B: Pull emphasis with added grip work
  1) Warm-up
  2) Lat pulldown (neutral grip) 4 x 8–10
  3) Seated row or incline row 4 x 8–10
  4) Dumbbell rear delt flys 3 x 12–15
  5) Farmer's carry or suitcase carry with light dumbbells for grip 3 x 30–45 seconds
  6) Core: dead bug progressions 3 x 12–15
  7) Mobility: doorway stretch, thoracic rotation 2 x 30s

- Day C: Push with limited ROM range extension and rotator cuff care
  1) Warm-up
  2) Dumbbell incline press: 4 x 8–10
  3) Push-ups on elevated surface or machine chest press: 3 x 10–12
  4) Cable cross-over or banded chest fly in a safe range: 3 x 12–15
  5) External rotation at 0–45 degrees external rotation: 3 x 12–15
  6) Scapular push-ups or wall slides: 3 x 12–15
  7) Mobility: lats/pec minor stretches 2 x 30s

- Progression cues Phase 2:
  - Increase external load modestly while preserving pain-free ROM.
  - Add 1–2 sets to main lifts if form remains solid and there’s no pain.

Phase 3 (Weeks 7–9): Strength focus with more challenging loading and early climbing transfer
 goals: push closer to maximal strength ranges with careful management of impingement; increase grip and pulling strength relevant to climbing.
 Weekly template (3 days)
- Day A: Horizontal push/pull emphasis
  1) Warm-up
  2) Bench press or floor press: 5 x 5 at a controlled tempo
  3) Barbell or supported row: 4 x 6–8
  4) Weighted incline press (light incline, careful not to flare): 3 x 6–8
  5) Band pull-aparts and face pulls: 3 x 15
  6) Pallof press or anti-rotational carry: 3 x 12
  7) Mobility: thoracic mobility sequence

- Day B: Pulling strength, grip, and rotator cuff
  1) Warm-up
  2) Weighted pull-ups or lat pull-downs: 4 x 6–8 (use band guidance if needed)
  3) Seated row or chest-supported row: 4 x 6–8
  4) Dumbbell shrugs with controlled tempo: 3 x 10–12
  5) Farmer’s carry: 3 x 40–60 seconds
  6) External rotation at 0–30 degrees: 3 x 12–15
  7) Mobility: scapular stabilization drills

- Day C: Push with control and climbing transfer
  1) Warm-up
  2) Push-up with elevated feet on incline: 4 x 10–12 or decline to adjust
  3) Dumbbell bench press with neutral grip: 4 x 6–8
  4) Cable or dumbbell lateral raises to 90 degrees with light weight (if tolerated): 3 x 12
  5) Internal rotation exercises 3 x 12–15
  6) Core: anti-rotation planks 3 x 20–30 seconds per side

- Progression cues Phase 3:
  - Increase loads on main lifts by small increments (2–5%) if technique is solid and pain remains absent.
  - Maintain pain-free ROM; if pain appears, revert to Phase 2 loads or reduce ROM.

Phase 4 (Weeks 10–12): Consolidation, climbing-specific strength, and conditioning
 goals: maximize strength while maintaining tendon health; integrate climbing-relevant loading (pulls, grip endurance) with minimal overhead stress.
 Weekly template (3 days)
- Day A: Strength upper body
  1) Warm-up
  2) Floor or close-grip bench press: 4 x 6–8
  3) Barbell row or chest-supported row: 4 x 6–8
  4) Cable face pulls: 3 x 12–15
  5) Pallof press: 3 x 12 (per side)
  6) Grip work: plate pinches or fat grips: 2 x 20–30 seconds
  7) Mobility: thoracic extension

- Day B: Climbing-specific pulling + scapular control
  1) Warm-up
  2) Lat pulldown (neutral grip) to chest height: 4 x 6–8
  3) Seated row: 4 x 8–10
  4) Inverted rows or low rows: 3 x 8–12
  5) Rotator cuff external/internal rotations: 3 x 12–15
  6) Core: dead bug or suitcase deadlift variation 3 x 12
  7) Mobility: thoracic spine flossing + pec stretch

- Day C: Push with improved tolerance
  1) Warm-up
  2) Dumbbell bench press with controlled ROM: 4 x 6–8
  3) Dumbbell incline press: 3 x 8–10
  4) Push-up tempo work (slow eccentrics): 3 x 6–8
  5) External rotation at 0–45 degrees: 3 x 12–15
  6) Core/anti-rotation: pallof press 3 x 12

- Deload week or autoregulation: If any day feels off during Week 12, reduce volume by 30–40% and maintain technique.

General weekly progression and loading plan
- Week 1–3: establish baselines with light–moderate loads, focus on technique and scapular control.
- Week 4–6: increase volume a bit; add sets and modest load increases on main lifts.
- Week 7–9: push closer to strength ranges (5 x 5, or 4–5 x 6–8) with careful monitoring for pain.
- Week 10–12: refine strength, emphasize climbing-specific patterns (pulls, rows, grip) while protecting the shoulder.

Accessory and conditioning
- Mobility and mobility maintenance: daily 5–10 minutes focusing on thoracic spine, scapular mobility, and pec/lat length.
- Climbing transfer work: 1–2 short sessions per week focusing on grip endurance (dead hangs minimal, if cleared by physio) and pulling mechanics; avoid overhead loading beyond pain-free ROM.
- Recovery: prioritize sleep (7–9 hours), hydration, and protein intake (~1.6–2.0 g/kg/day). Include post-workout nutrition with a mix of protein and carbohydrates.
- Nutritional guidance: maintain energy balance aligned with training demands; ensure adequate protein distribution across meals. If weight goals exist, adjust caloric intake gradually with monitoring.
- Injury management: continue any physio protocols; if pain worsens or swelling occurs, revert to Phase 1 levels and consult clinician.

Notes on exercise substitutions
- If any exercise triggers pain: switch to machine-based pressing/pulling with neutral grip, reduce ROM, or use lighter loads. Replace overhead pressing with machine press variations or push-tull positions in neutral, and emphasize scapular stabilization.
- If the client has limited grip strength: incorporate isometric holds and farmer’s carries earlier and progress gradually.

Example weekly schedule (illustrative)
- Monday: Day A (horizontal push/pull + scapular focus)
- Wednesday: Day B (pull emphasis + grip)
- Friday: Day C (push with rotator cuff care)
- Optional Saturday: mobility/technique drill or climbing-specific endurance circuit (low intensity, no pain)

Progress tracking
- Record pain level (0–10), ROM, and strength for key lifts weekly.
- Track load and reps for main lifts; target consistent improvements without pain.
- Reassess every 3 weeks with functional checks (scapular control, ROM in pain-free range, ability to perform climbing movements without pain).

This plan is designed to progressively increase upper-body strength while respecting the client’s subacromial impingement. If you’d like, I can tailor exact exercise substitutions, set/rep schemes, and load targets based on her current 1RM estimates, climbing schedule, and available equipment.

Here’s a concise, actionable nutrition plan to accompany the 12-week upper-body program, tailored for body recomposition (lose fat subtly while gaining or preserving lean mass) for a 29-year-old recreational climber with subacromial impingement. It assumes a generally active climber with 3 days of upper-body strength work, some climbing, and daily activities. Key aims: modest caloric balance, adequate protein, strategic carbohydrate timing around training, healthy fats, and hydration. Include adjustments every 2–3 weeks based on progress, energy, and recovery.

1) Calorie targets (starting point)
- Estimate maintenance calories: use a quick calculator or typical ranges for a 29-year-old, 5’5”–5’8” female/male? Since the client’s sex isn’t specified, provide a flexible approach. Use bodyweight-based ranges as starting point:
  - If female: maintenance ~ 28–32 kcal per kg bodyweight per day.
  - If male: maintenance ~ 30–34 kcal per kg bodyweight per day.
- For body recomposition with training: start at maintenance or at a slight deficit of 200–300 kcal/day if energy and recovery allow.
- Target pace: aim for 0.25–0.5% bodyweight change per week. If goal is lean mass preservation or slight gain with fat loss, hold at maintenance with precise protein and resistance training to favor muscle retention.

2) Macronutrient targets (daily)
- Protein: 1.6–2.2 g per kg bodyweight per day. This supports muscle repair, tendon health, and satiety. For example, a 65 kg person would target 104–143 g/day.
- Carbohydrates: 3–5 g per kg bodyweight per day, adjusted to training load. On heavier climbing or lifting days, aim closer to 4–5 g/kg; on lighter days, 3–4 g/kg.
- Fats: 0.8–1.0 g per kg bodyweight per day as a baseline, focusing on unsaturated fats.
- Fiber: 25–38 g/day depending on tolerance and gut health.

3) Meal timing and composition (practical strategy)
- Pre-workout meal (60–90 minutes before): moderate carbs + protein, low fat to aid digestion. Example: yogurt with berries and a small handful of oats; or a banana with peanut butter and a protein shake (if tolerated).
- Post-workout: prioritize protein and carbs within 1–2 hours to support recovery. Example: shake with 20–30 g protein + 40–60 g fast-dacting carbs (fruit, honey, rice cakes) or a balanced meal (chicken, rice, veggies).
- Regular meals: distribute protein across 3–5 meals to maximize muscle protein synthesis (aim ~25–40 g protein per meal depending on total daily target).
- Evening snack (if training late or hungry): casein protein, Greek yogurt, or cottage cheese to support overnight recovery.

4) Hydration and performance
- Water: at least 2.5–3.5 L/day for most adults; adjust based on sweat rate and climate.
- Electrolytes: if climbing sessions are long or hot, include sodium during workouts (e.g., 300–600 mg Na per hour) and maintain a salty taste if needed.
- Caffeine: up to 300 mg/day, if tolerated, 30–60 minutes pre-workout for performance; avoid late-day caffeine if sleep is impacted.

5) Nutrient timing guidelines for recovery and tendon health
- Emphasize leucine-rich protein sources (chicken, fish, eggs, dairy, legumes) to maximize muscle protein synthesis.
- Include omega-3 fatty acids (2–3 servings/week of fatty fish or 1–2 g/day of EPA/DHA supplement if dietary intake is low) for inflammation modulation and tendon health.
- Include vitamin C and zinc-rich foods to support tissue repair (citrus, berries, peppers, beef, shellfish, legumes).
- Ensure adequate vitamin D and calcium for bone and connective tissue health, especially if gym exposure is indoor/climbing-related.

6) Sample day plan (example for a 70 kg climber)
- Breakfast: 3 eggs + 2 egg whites, spinach, tomatoes; 1 cup oatmeal with berries; coffee.
- Snack: Greek yogurt with honey and almonds.
- Lunch: grilled chicken (150 g) + quinoa (1 cup cooked) + mixed vegetables + olive oil (1–2 tbsp).
- Pre-workout: banana + protein shake (20–25 g protein).
- Post-workout: protein shake (25 g) + rice cakes (2–3) with jam or honey.
- Dinner: salmon (150 g) + sweet potato (1 medium) + broccoli + avocado.
- Evening: cottage cheese or casein (20–30 g) if needed to meet daily protein target.

7) Supplements to consider (optional, discuss with clinician)
- Protein powder to help meet daily protein targets if whole foods are insufficient.
- Creatine monohydrate: 3–5 g/day may support strength and tendon adaptation; ensure hydration and assess any GI tolerance.
- Vitamin D3 if deficient or insufficient sun exposure (dosage per clinician recommendation).
- Magnesium before bed if cramps or sleep disrupted (ensure not interfering with other meds).

8) Week-by-week nutrition adjustments (align with training phases)
- Phase 1 (Weeks 1–3): set protein target, monitor energy; if fatigue or training quality declines, adjust to maintenance with adequate protein. Keep a slight deficit only if energy and recovery are good.
- Phase 2 (Weeks 4–6): support increased training volume by ensuring adequate carbs around sessions; slight bump in calories on heavier lifting days (~100–150 kcal) if performance wanes.
- Phase 3 (Weeks 7–9): maintain or slightly increase calories if climbing sessions intensify; prioritize carbs around climbing days; emphasize timing to support muscle synthesis.
- Phase 4 (Weeks 10–12): align with strength gains and any climbing volume; maintain protein; balance carbs to fuel sessions; consider a small deficit only if fat loss is desired and recovery is solid.

9) Practical tracking and adjustment
- Track daily calories and protein for at least 2 weeks to establish habit and observe trends.
- Monitor bodyweight 2–3 times per week (same time of day, similar conditions) and adjust calories if weight is changing more than 0.25–0.5% per week.
- Track training performance, energy, sleep, and recovery; if performance declines or injury risk rises, adjust calories up (increase 150–250 kcal/day) and ensure protein remains high.
- Use a simple plate method: protein 1 palm (size), carbs 1 cupped handful, fats 1 thumb, veggies as desired.

10) Safety and caveats
- If the client has any metabolic, medical, or hormonal conditions, or is underweight or under a physician’s care, adjust under supervision.
- For subacromial impingement, ensure nutrition supports tendon health without encouraging inflammation; limit highly processed foods, added sugars, and trans fats when possible to support overall recovery.

The cardio pieces will be low-to-moderate intensity, climb-relevant, and designed not to provoke shoulder irritation or interfere with strength work. I’ll provide options for days, modalities, durations, and how to periodize across phases.

Overall approach
- Cardio goals: improve aerobic base, work capacity for long climbing days, aid recovery, and support body recomposition goals.
- Modalities: a mix of steady-state cardio and climbing-specific conditioning (when available), plus optional tempo/zone 2 sessions.
- Scheduling: 2x/week on non-consecutive days, separated from high-intensity upper-body lifting by at least 24 hours when possible. If climbing days are scheduled, cardio can be integrated as light warm-up or active recovery rather than a separate session.

Phase-aligned cardio plan (weeks 1–12)
Phase 1 (Weeks 1–3): Establish base and low-stress conditioning
- Option 1: Steady-state cardio
  - 1 session: 30–40 minutes at conversational pace (Zone 2) on a cycle, treadmill incline walk, or elliptical.
  - Focus on keeping shoulders relaxed; avoid aggressive arm pump.
- Option 2: Climbing-specific cardio (if gym allows)
  - 2 rounds of 10–12 minutes on easy-climb routes with long rest between attempts; emphasize steady, controlled pacing and technical efficiency rather than max effort.
- Session placement: Preferably on a non-lifting day or after a light upper-body day with 24+ hours before the next heavy session.

Phase 2 (Weeks 4–6): Build endurance and work capacity
- Session 1: Zone 2 cardio 35–45 minutes continuous or broken into two 20–22 minute efforts with a short 2–3 minute break, maintaining RPE 4–6/10.
- Session 2: Climbing-relevant cardio
  - “Endurance blocks” on the wall: 4–6 sets of 4–6 minutes climbing at a steady, sub-maximal pace with 2–3 minutes rest between sets. Emphasize efficient movement and breathing.
- Optional: Include 10–15 minutes of gentle post-climb mobility work.

Phase 3 (Weeks 7–9): Endurance density and recovery balance
- Session 1: Longer cardio piece
  - 40–50 minutes at Zone 2, or 2 x 20–25 minutes with a short 2–4 minute rest, focusing on aerobic efficiency.
- Session 2: Climbing endurance sequence
  - 3–4 rounds of 6–8 minutes on easier routes, with 2 minutes rest; aim for smooth, clipped-in endurance rather than high-intensity bouldery effort.
- If peak climbing volume is high, consider reducing cardio duration by 10–15 minutes to protect recovery.

Phase 4 (Weeks 10–12): Peak endurance modulation
- Session 1: Interval-like but endurance-oriented
  - 2–3 intervals: 3–4 minutes at a strong, steady pace (RPE 7/10) with 2 minutes easy pace between; total 18–22 minutes of work.
  - This keeps conditioning without overtaxing joints.
- Session 2: Climbing-focused endurance day
  - 4–6 blocks of 6–8 minutes on moderate routes with 2–3 minutes rest, plus a final boulder-finish circuit (optional) if shoulders tolerate it.

General cardio progression cues
- If fatigue accumulates, reduce volume by 20–30% for a week and reassess.
- Always prioritize technique and shoulder comfort; if any pain appears, drop intensity or duration until pain-free.
- Keep cardio intensity below the threshold that exacerbates impingement; avoid sustained high-velocity arm movements in warm-up.

Integration with upper-body plan and nutrition
- Schedule: Place cardio sessions away from the most demanding upper-body lifting days. A practical layout could be:
  - Monday: Upper-body Day A

Here is the integrated 12-week upper-body strength program with all the adjustments we’ve made: phase structure, weekly layout, exercises, sets/reps, progression, nutrition basics, cardio, hangboard/climbing prep, mobility, and the Saturday Finisher Day. It’s designed for a 29-year-old recreational climber with right subacromial impingement, pain-free ROM only, no overhead loading, full gym access, and a goal of climbing performance with body recomposition.

Assumptions and scaffolding
- Training days: 4 days/week upper-body-focused (Mon, Tue, Fri) plus a cardio day and a Saturday Finisher Day (extra optional). Hangboard and climbing prep are integrated in Phases 3–4. Cardio 2x/week is included from earlier plans. Mobility routines are integrated daily or as part of warm-ups/cool-downs.
- Phase structure: 4 phases, each 3 weeks (Phase 1: Weeks 1–3; Phase 2: Weeks 4–6; Phase 3: Weeks 7–9; Phase 4: Weeks 10–12). Phase 3 emphasizes a peak in pushing strength with a taper into Phase 4 for climbing peak.
- Load and technique: pain-free ROM only; scapular control emphasized; no overhead pressing beyond pain-free ROM; use neutral grips and controlled tempos to protect tendons.

Phase 1 (Weeks 1–3): Foundation and scapular stability
Goals: establish scapular motor control, rotator cuff endurance, and pain-free loading. Build confidence with loading in pain-free ranges; set baselines.

Weekly template (3 days; Day A, B, C)
- Day A: Horizontal pushing/pulling + scapular control
  - Warm-up: scapular band pull-aparts 2x15; sidelying external rotation 2x12 per side; thoracic mobility 2x8 per side
  - Dumbbell floor/flat bench press: 3x10–12 (tempo 3–0-1-0; light)
  - Supported row (chest-supported or prone): 3x8–12
  - Seated cable face pulls: 3x12–15
  - Neutral-grip anti-rotational press or short ROM neutral press: 2–3x8–10
  - Core: dead bug or Pallof press 3x10–12
  - Mobility finish: lat stretch 2x30s; pec minor stretch 2x30s
- Day B: Pulling emphasis + scapular focus
  - Warm-up as above
  - Lat pulldown neutral/supinated to chest height (pain-free): 3x8–10
  - Seated row or incline row: 3x8–12
  - Dumbbell rear delt row or band pull-aparts: 3x12
  - Prone Y raises: 2x12
  - Pallof press or anti-rotation carry: 3x12 each side
  - Mobility: doorway pec stretch 2x30s; thoracic extension on foam roller 2x1min
- Day C: Push with control and cuff care
  - Warm-up: shoulder activation
  - Push-up variation on elevated surface or machine press: 3x8–12
  - Dumbbell incline press (limited ROM): 3x8–12
  - Cable/band internal/external rotation at 0–45°: 3x12–15
  - Scapular push-ups or wall slides: 3x12–15
  - Anti-rotator cuff work with band: 2x10
  - Mobility: scapular wall slides 2x10; doorway stretch 2x30s
- Progression cues Phase 1:
  - Increase total volume gradually if pain-free; small load increases weekly on main lifts; stay in ~75–80% effort for main lifts.
  - If any pain arises with overhead components, regress to neutral grips, reduced ROM, or machine-based options.

Phase 2 (Weeks 4–6): Building strength with controlled progression
Goals: increase loading with safe overload, refine scapular mechanics, more pulling volume.

Weekly template (3 days)
- Day A: Horizontal push/pull + scapular stability
  - Warm-up: as Phase 1 plus banded scapular pulls
  - Bench press or floor press: 4x6–8 (tempo 3–0-1-0; moderate weight)
  - Bent-over barbell row or chest-supported row: 4x6–8
  - Inverted row or supported T-bar row: 3x8–12
  - Cable face pulls: 3x12–15
  - Pallof press: 3x12 each side
  - Mobility: thoracic mobility sequence
- Day B: Pull emphasis with grip work
  - Warm-up
  - Lat pulldown neutral: 4x8–10
  - Seated row or incline row: 4x8–10
  - Dumbbell rear delt flys: 3x12–15
  - Farmer’s carry or suitcase carry: 3x40–45s
  - Core: dead bug progressions 3x12–15
  - Mobility: doorway stretch; thoracic rotation 2x30s
- Day C: Push with limited ROM extension and cuff care
  - Warm-up
  - Dumbbell incline press: 4x8–10
  - Push-ups on elevated surface or machine chest press: 3x10–12
  - Cable cross or band chest fly in safe ROM: 3x12–15
  - External rotation at 0–45°: 3x12–15
  - Scapular push-ups or wall slides: 3x12–15
  - Mobility: lat/pec lengthening
- Progression cues Phase 2:
  - Increase external load modestly while preserving pain-free ROM.
  - Add 1–2 sets to main lifts if form solid and pain-free.

Phase 3 (Weeks 7–9): Peak push strength with climb-focused taper; hangboard prep begins
Goals: peak pushing strength while preserving tendon health; begin climb-specific loading with hangboard introduction in late Phase 3.

Phase 3 revised template (to peak for climbing in Week 12)
- Day A: Horizontal push/pull with peak strength focus
  - Warm-up: scapular activation; light single-arm press drill for stability
  - Bench press or floor press: 5x5 at ~85% of 5RM, tempo 3–0-1-0
  - Barbell row or supported row: 4x6–8
  - Weighted incline press: 3x6–8 (moderate incline; avoid flare)
  - Face pulls: 3x12–15
  - Pallof press: 3x12
  - Mobility: thoracic/shoulder work
- Day B: Pulling strength with shoulder health
  - Warm-up
  - Weighted pull-ups or lat pulldowns: 4x6–8
  - Seated row or incline row: 4x6–8
  - Dumbbell rear delt flys: 3x12
  - Farmer’s carry or suitcase carry: 3x40–60s
  - External rotation 0–30°: 3x12–15
  - Mobility: scapular drills
- Day C: Push with high-intensity and climb prep
  - Warm-up
  - Push-ups with elevated feet on incline: 4x6–8
  - Dumbbell bench press with neutral grip: 4x6–8
  - Pallof press: 3x12
  - External rotation 0–45°: 3x12–15
  - Core: anti-rotation planks 3x20–30s per side
- Hangboard and climbing prep (Phase 3)
  - Hangboard: 1x/week consistently (2x in Weeks 9 if tolerance is good)
    - 2–3 sets of 6–8s hangs on a comfortable edge, 4–6s rest
    - Optional 1–2 sets of 6–8s half-crimp hangs if tolerated; otherwise stick to open-hand
    - 2–3 minutes rest between sets; total session 15–25s
  - Climbing-specific prep: 20–30 minutes on easy routes, technique focus; scapular circuits 5–10 minutes
- Weekly push progression cues Weeks 7–9
  - Week 7: 5x5 at ~85% 5RM for main press; other lifts at prescribed reps
  - Week 8: +2–4% load if form solid; keep 5x5 or drop to 4x6 if needed
  - Week 9: Peak week for main press on Day A (e.g., 5x4 at near 90% 5RM if tolerated); lighter Day C 4x6 at 75–80%

Phase 4 (Weeks 10–12): Taper and peak climbing performance
Goals: maintain peak strength while reducing fatigue, maximize climbing performance with climbing-specific focus, as planed.

Phase 4 template (3 days + climbing/hangboard + finisher)
- Day A: Upper-body strength maintenance with lighter loads
  - Floor press or close-grip bench: 3x5–6 at 70–75% 1RM
  - Barbell row: 3x6–8
  - Face pulls: 3x12
  - Pallof press: 3x12
  - Grip work: plate pinches or fat grips: 2x20–30s
- Day B: Climbing pulling endurance
  - Lat pulldown to chest height: 3–4x6–8
  - Seated row or incline row: 3–4x6–8
  - Inverted rows: 3x6–8
- Day C: Push with technique and control
  - Neutral-grip dumbbell bench: 3x6–8
  - Push-ups (controlled tempo): 3x10–12
  - External rotation 3x12–15
- Hangboard and climbing prep (Phase 4)
  - Hangboard 1–2x/week if finger health permits
    - Week 10: 3x6–8s on comfortable edge, 4–6s rest; 1 neg hang if tolerated
    - Week 11: 3–4x6–10s; 1–2 neg hangs if tolerated
    - Week 12: Optional micro-loads or maintain Week 11 level
  - Climbing endurance blocks: 2–3 sessions weekly
    - 2–4 blocks of 6–8 minutes on moderate routes; 2 minutes rest; add light traverses
- Saturday Finisher Day (still in Phase 4 if desired)
  - 45–60 minutes full-body finisher (as described earlier) with reduced volume if climbing/training fatigue is high
- Taper specifics
  - Week 10: 90% of Week 9 intensity; 20–30% volume reduction
  - Week 11: 70–75% of Week 9; maintain technique emphasis
  - Week 12: Minimal effective stress; 1 light upper-body session midweek; extended warm-up for climbing
- Climbing-specific peaking considerations
  - Emphasize technique, movement quality, route reading, and endurance, not max strength.
  - Ensure nutrition supports climbing energy needs on heavy days; adjust carbs around climbing.

Nutrition and cardio integration (high level)
- Calorie targets: maintenance or slight deficit for body recomposition, protein 1.6–2.2 g/kg/day; carbs higher on climbing and lifting days; fats 0.8–1.0 g/kg/day.
- Protein distribution: 25–40 g per meal across 3–5 meals; include leucine-rich sources.
- Hydration: 2.5–3.5 L/day; electrolytes for long sessions.
- Supplements (optional): protein powder, creatine 3–5 g/day, vitamin D if needed.

Mobility and recovery
- Daily mobility: 5–15 minutes; thoracic mobility, scapular control, shoulder capsule health, hip/ankle mobility
- Pre-climb warm-up: 2–3 minutes of thoracic extension, scapular activation, band pull-aparts
- Post-climb mobility: 3–5 minutes chest/lat opening, thoracic extension, breathing work
- Sleep targets: 7–9 hours; prioritize sleep for recovery and performance

Saturday Finisher Day (fully integrated)
- 45–60 minutes; full-body, low-to-moderate intensity; 3 circuits focusing on conditioning, grip, core, and movement quality
- Integrated as optional depending on fatigue; can be bypassed on climbing-heavy weeks

Weekly example (illustrative)
- Week 1 (Phase 1)
  - Mon Day A; Tue Cardio Zone 2; Wed Day B; Thu Mobility; Fri Day C; Sat Rest or mobility; Sun Climbing or off
- Week 4 (Phase 2)
  - Mon Day A; Tue Cardio Zone 2; Wed Day B; Thu Mobility; Fri Day C; Sat Finisher (optional); Sun Rest
- Week 7 (Phase 3 start)
  - Mon Day A (5x5 at ~85%); Tue Cardio Zone 2 or climb prep; Wed Day B; Thu Mobility; Fri Day C; Sat Hangboard (Week 7: 1x); Sun Rest
- Week 9 (Phase 3 peak)
  - Mon Day A heavy; Tue Cardio low; Wed Day B moderate; Thu Mobility; Fri Day C; Sat Hangboard (if tolerance allows); Sun Rest
- Week 10–12 (Phase 4 taper)
  - Follow Phase 4 structure; reduce volume; ensure peak readiness for climbing trip; adjust hangboard and climbing sessions as needed

Notes and adjustments
- If pain flares: regress back to Phase 1–2 loads; prioritize scapular control and ROM; avoid any overhead loading beyond pain-free ROM.
- If fatigue is high, autoregulate using RPE and reduce sets/reps to maintain form and minimize tendon load.

- Weekly check-ins: track pain, ROM, performance in lifts, climbing ability, energy, and sleep. Adjust phase transitions, volumes, and the schedule if needed.
